{"id": "2:144/q57", "question": "Is the qibla the Kaaba's structure or its occupied space?", "turns_on": "Whether the qibla survives demolition as spatial location rather than material structure.", "positions": [{"id": "2:144/q57/p1", "position": "The qibla is the space occupied by the Kaaba, surviving demolition.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Razi concludes that the qibla is the empty spatial volume occupied by the Kaaba, rather than the material building. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The name al-Masjid al-Haram refers to the constructed building, while its direction is the particular space occupied by that building; thus the verse points to the empty space as qibla."}, {"id": "2:144/q57/p2", "position": "The physical building constitutes the qibla.", "reasons": "Against: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The qibla cannot be just the Kaaba's physical stones and timber: moving its rubble elsewhere and rebuilding would not make the new structure a qibla. Against: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The qibla is not the building together with its original location, since after demolition and removal the cleared site remains the direction for worshippers elsewhere."}]}
{"id": "2:144/q58", "question": "May one pray on the Kaaba's roof or its cleared site?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:144/q58/p1", "position": "Prayer from the cleared Kaaba site is valid.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): If the Kaaba were demolished, Razi prefers Ibn Surayj's and Abu Hanifa's view that prayer from its site is valid, over his own school's invalidity ruling, since the worshipper faces part of the qibla-space."}, {"id": "2:144/q58/p2", "position": "Prayer on the roof is valid even without a wall in front.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Razi likewise chooses Ibn Surayj's view that prayer on the Kaaba's roof is valid even without a wall in front, because the worshipper faces the qibla-space."}]}
{"id": "2:144/q59", "question": "Must one separately intend facing the qibla?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:144/q59/p1", "position": "No separate intention to face the qibla is required.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): No separate intention to face the qibla is required: carrying out the commanded act suffices, as with covering the nakedness and purifying the place and clothing."}, {"id": "2:144/q59/p2", "position": "One must intend the Kaaba itself while facing its general direction.", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (أبو حنيفة وأحمد وأكثر الخراسانيين من الشافعية): Even those who require facing the Kaaba's direction say the worshipper must intend the Kaaba itself as the qibla."}]}
{"id": "2:144/q60", "question": "What does qibla inference imply for legal reasoning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:144/q60/p1", "position": "The qibla rule is cited as proof of legal analogy.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (الشافعي): Shafi'i uses this reasoning to argue that analogical reasoning is a valid proof in religious law. Against: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Razi rejects the proof because it would establish analogy by another analogy, which he says is not valid."}, {"id": "2:144/q60/p2", "position": "The qibla rule warrants legal reliance on well-grounded conjecture.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The command to face the qibla, together with the need for ijtihad to identify it and the rule that necessary means are obligatory, makes ijtihad obligatory; since it rests on co\n\n\n\nnjecture, the verse establishes legal reliance on conjecture."}]}
{"id": "2:144/q61", "question": "What spelling or written form is noted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:144/q61/p1", "position": "Haythu and ma are written as two words.", "reasons": "NASHR, d. 833 (author): The two-word sequence haythu ma is written separately wherever it occurs."}, {"id": "2:144/q61/p2", "position": "The spelling of Ibrahim without ya in al-Baqara is noted.", "reasons": "SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT (author): The spelling of إبراهيم without yā in al-Baqarah is an issue of Qur’anic orthography that the program had discussed in detail in earlier episodes."}]}
{"id": "2:144/q62", "question": "How can hearers recognize truth yet resist it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:144/q62/p1", "position": "Quraysh recognized the Quran's force while publicly resisting it.", "reasons": "BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 (author): The Quraysh listeners returned on later nights despite agreeing not to; they listened until dawn, met by chance, reproached one another, and renewed their resolve. BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 (السيرة): The Quraysh leaders sent ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa to negotiate; after hearing verses from Fuṣṣilat, he returned visibly captivated, prompting their remark that he was changed. BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 (author): Though Quraysh called the Qur’an poetry, sorcery, or soothsaying, they knew it was none of these and recognized its extraordinary hold over minds and hearts. BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 (author): Before the pilgrimage season, Quraysh leaders planned to block routes to Mecca and agreed on a single account of the Qur’an so visiting tribes would not hear conflicting descriptions."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q01", "question": "How is 'those who' parsed in relation to the patient?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative noun remains a modifier, is cut off for praise, or begins a new sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q01/p1", "position": "It qualifies 'the patient' as an accusative adjective.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī reports it; Abū Ḥayyān lists it; al-Samīn prefers it."}, {"id": "2:156/q01/p2", "position": "It is a new subject whose predicate is 'upon them are blessings' in 2:157.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Samīn place the intervening conditional in the relative clause."}, {"id": "2:156/q01/p3", "position": "It is an accusative expression of praise.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report the accusative cut-off for commendation."}, {"id": "2:156/q01/p4", "position": "It is nominative after an omitted 'they are', as a detached or resumed construction.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn supply hum; al-Samīn allows both cut-off and new resumption."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q02", "question": "What does 'when' imply about the occurrence of calamity?", "turns_on": "Whether idhā itself conveys repetition.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q02/p1", "position": "It indicates a general, recurring condition.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says idhā here denotes repetition and notes grammarians dispute whether the particle itself requires recurrence."}, {"id": "2:156/q02/p2", "position": "The particle can mark a single occurrence.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the opposing grammatical view, though he reads this instance generally."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q03", "question": "What counts as a 'calamity' here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is restricted to severe personal injury or includes every painful loss.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q03/p1", "position": "Any unpleasant harm that befalls a believer, however small, including loss affecting self, family, or property.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says it never names good fortune; al-Qurṭubī includes the slightest evil and cites illness, fatigue, sorrow, and anxiety in Muslim. The extinguished lamp, thorn, mosquito bite, and broken sandal strap illustrate breadth in Kashshāf, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ālūsī. Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, and Abū Ḥayyān specify person, family, and possessions. Bursawī derives it from reaching its target; Biqāʿī notes that the root striking a mark can describe what pleases or displeases although this occurrence is a loss. Ibn ʿĀshūr refers its lexical discussion to 4:72."}, {"id": "2:156/q03/p2", "position": "It is severe harm to the self.", "reasons": "Jishumī derives muṣība from iṣāba, as though the injury strikes a person; Ṭabrisī likewise speaks of hardship striking the soul."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q04", "question": "How are the forms and plurals of muṣība explained?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural hamza follows mistaken pattern analogy or a direct sound substitution.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q04/p1", "position": "The yāʾ in muṣība is a root letter replacing wāw; hamzated maṣāʾib arose by mistaken analogy.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī explains that speakers treated root yāʾ as a lengthening yāʾ, as in safīna/safāʾin and ṣaḥīfa/ṣaḥāʾif. He quotes Sībawayh calling the hamza an error, Abū ʿAlī preferring this account for its parallels, and Abū al-Ḥasan's comparable masīl plural. Al-Qurṭubī says Arab usage consistently hamzates the plural despite its original radical. The forms muṣāb, muṣāba, and muṣawba occur in al-Farrāʾ's poetry, al-Kisāʾī's Bedouin example, and al-Qurṭubī's verse about an unjust tribute; al-Qurṭubī adds the dialectal ṣāba for aṣāba."}, {"id": "2:156/q04/p2", "position": "The hamza of maṣāʾib directly replaces a kasra wāw.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī reports Abū Isḥāq's comparison with isāda; Abū ʿAlī rejects it because no parallel changes a noninitial kasra wāw in this way."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q05", "question": "Why does the verse say that a calamity 'strikes them'?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary rhetorical effects, sound pairing and unassigned agency.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q05/p1", "position": "The verb and noun make a paronomastic pairing.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān compares similarly paired words in 53:57 and 56:1."}, {"id": "2:156/q05/p2", "position": "The wording leaves the agent unnamed so it covers harms from God and from people.", "reasons": "Al-Qāḍī in Rāzī and al-Muntakhab in Abū Ḥayyān distinguish divine causes from human ones; Rāzī illustrates fear by drowning, fire, lightning, or hostile Arabs, hunger by destroyed or seized wealth, property loss by disaster or enemy pressure, and death by dying or killing."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q06", "question": "What kind of hardship is in view in the passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the trials are read broadly or chiefly through the coming communal conflict.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q06/p1", "position":

Al-Qāḍī says duties remain in either case."}, {"id": "2:156/q06/p2", "position": "The immediate setting anticipates a collective trial of conflict for monotheism and battle.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the five verses came before the legislation of jihad, after opponents had exhausted other means; collective distress impairs common judgment and planning. The passage presents death in God's path as life and patience and prayer as protection."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q07", "question": "How does 'they say' function in the construction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q07/p1", "position": "The quoted declaration is the response to idhā within the relative clause.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān specifies qālū innā lillāh as the conditional response."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q08", "question": "How may 'innā lillāh' be pronounced?", "turns_on": "Whether the kasra and frequent formulaic use license imāla here.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q08/p1", "position": "Imāla inclines its alif toward kasra in some transmissions from al-Kisāʾī.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās attributes permission to al-Kisāʾī; Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, al-Jazarī, and al-Suyūṭī locate the inclination in innā and/or lillāh. The following kasra, the divine name, and frequent use make the sequence nearly one word; al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī exclude innā before other names. Qutayba's transmission limits it to innā lillāh, not wa-innā ilayhi. Al-Jazarī surveys broader triggers: neighboring or underlying kasra and yāʾ, rhyme, resemblance, and frequent use; al-Suyūṭī reduces the causes to resemblance and indication and gives further examples."}, {"id": "2:156/q08/p2", "position": "It may be pronounced with full tafkhīm.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās expressly permits it; Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, and Rāzī say other readers use it."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q09", "question": "What explains the form innā?", "turns_on": "Whether the apparent vowel is analyzed as morphological contraction or through formulaic fusion; Naḥḥās objects to the latter account.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q09/p1", "position": "It contracts from innanā by dropping one nūn for ease while retaining grammatical government.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās cites the same lightening in wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūn; Abū Ḥayyān says dropping the second identical nūn preserves the particle's operation."}, {"id": "2:156/q09/p2", "position": "In this grief formula, the nūn is said to take kasra through the following lām.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says frequency fuses the expression like one word and compares kāfir and al-ḥamdu lillāh. Naḥḥās rejects this as mistaken: the nūn is not kasra, and an alif cannot itself be vowelled."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q10", "question": "What do they acknowledge by saying 'we belong to God'?", "turns_on": "Whether the statement is explained as ownership and servitude or developed as inward surrender.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q10/p1", "position": "Their selves, families, possessions, and all they hold are God's property; they are His servants under His rightful disposal.", "reasons": "Zajjāj, Māwardī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, and others say ownership entails accepting His judgment. Māwardī says He does not wrong them; Jishumī and al-Qāḍī distinguish God's own acts from justice sought against human harm. Qushayrī says the Creator has greater claim; Bursawī says His gifts are His favor and reclaimed things are stored for the servant. Biqāʿī says God encompasses all things. Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues human possession is only apparent by divine permission, citing 40:16; Study Quran relates the claim to 2:116, 2:255, and 2:284. Ali and al-Warrāq distinguish this ownership confession from the second clause's mortality."}, {"id": "2:156/q10/p2", "position": "It is an inward surrender that witnesses God's power and accepts His allotment beyond personal choice.", "reasons": "Al-Qāsim says every ordeal hides blessing and even its blessing hides love's fire; neither piety nor disobedience reverses events. Qushayrī contrasts the one 'for God,' who remains patient, with the one 'by God,' who loses choice and judgment. Qāshānī sees God's continual disposal and manifestations of His attributes."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q11", "question": "What does 'to Him we return' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether return denotes resurrection and final judgment, sole divine rule, human annihilation, subsistence through God, compensation, or an inward effacement; spatial motion is explicitly rejected.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q11/p1", "position": "People die and are raised in the Hereafter for God's judgment, reward, or punishment.", "reasons": "Zajjāj stresses resurrection and reward for patience; Māwardī includes punishment of wrongdoers; Abū Ḥayyān calls death the greatest calamity, making lesser losses bearable. Ibn Kathīr says no atom of good is lost. Elmalılı includes gathering and a new creation after barzakh, distinguishes the ultimate Hereafter from the interval, and says people die bearing earned deeds; he links the contented soul's return to 89:27–28. Study Quran cites 2:210, 2:281, 3:83, and 5:48 for the wider motif."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p2", "position": "It is arrival at the Hereafter where God alone openly holds power to judge, benefit, and harm.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says temporary delegated human control ends. Jishumī reports the view that no other authority judges there. Rāzī compares returning sovereignty with returning power, not travel; Bursawī and Elmalılı also reject a spatial destination because God transcends place and direction."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p3", "position": "It acknowledges human death, passing away, or annihilation.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr al-Warrāq, Ali, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursawī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrast God's ownership in the first clause with human perishing in the second. Elmalılı lists this as one figurative possibility."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p4", "position": "Return involves both essential passing away and continued existence solely through God.", "reasons": "Elmalılı prefers this third reading over annihilation alone or subsistence alone. Divine knowledge preserves the person's reality even if body or soul perishes; 28:88 says all but God's Face perishes. God as universal cause and Living Sustainer can renew bodily or spiritual forms endlessly; the soul may survive barzakh but resurrection is a distinct new creation. People return bearing good or bad deeds and endure in a manifestation of beauty or majesty, with divine beauty the highest aim. He invokes 12:21 and the contented and pleasing soul of 89:27–28, and disputes making independent soul survival the foundation of the Hereafter."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p5", "position": "Return is understood as compensation of the loss and abundant reward from God.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this as a distinct explanation."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p6", "position": "Inwardly it means effacing the self in God and witnessing its annihilation in Him.", "reasons": "Qāshānī joins this reading to witnessing divine attributes through calamity."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p7", "position": "It refers to the soul's own continued spiritual existence as the basis of the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports philosophers using 'spiritual subsistence' this way, and reports the soul's continuation as an explanation of the interval after death; he objects that independent self-subsistence forgets God as First Cause."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p8", "position": "It is literal motion toward God in a place or direction.", "reasons": "Rāzī, Bursawī, and Elmalılı explicitly reject spatial movement as impossible for God."}, {"id": "2:156/q11/p9", "position": "Returning is a thing's restoration to a former state or ownership.", "reasons": "Jishumī links the root sense to 96:8; Ṭabrisī compares a house becoming someone's property again and calls it synonymous with returning and becoming."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q12", "question": "What relation do the two clauses bear to present and future affliction?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast is temporal, ownership versus mortality, or a joined confession of servitude and resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q12/p1", "position": "The first accepts the present loss; the second accepts the future, including final reward and redress.", "reasons": "Rāzī says both entrust affairs to God and encompass vindication from a wrongdoer; Abū Ḥayyān reports the present/future reading. Rāzī also links the latter with self-humbling and contentment with promised afterlife reward."}, {"id": "2:156/q12/p2", "position": "The first confesses ownership; the second confesses death or annihilation.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr al-Warrāq, Ali, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī give this pair of meanings; Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes a fuller version in al-Kāfī."}, {"id": "2:156/q12/p3", "position": "Together they confess servitude and resurrection, giving refuge and consolation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the words unite monotheism, servitude, resurrection, and certainty of God's final ownership; al-Qurṭubī calls them refuge and protection for the same reason. Kashshāf says the expression marks surrender and acquiescence."}]}

Wāḥidī cites the Prophet that patience is at the first blow; Ālūsī also stresses the first shock. Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī say patience requires inward recognition of life's purpo

se, the greater remaining blessings, and the final return. Ibn ʿĀshūr says empty recitation gains no merit, but speaking conviction reinforces it and teaches others. Ibn Masʿūd says falling from the sky would be preferable to wishing that God's decree had not happened."}, {"id": "2:156/q13/p2", "position": "Where people cause the harm, the believer seeks God's justice while restraining anger and unlawful retaliation.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Qāḍī in Rāzī distinguish this from accepting a God-sent affliction as wise, good, and beneficial; the words commit the sufferer to God's just command in both cases. Rāzī cites 40:20 for God's right judgment."}, {"id": "2:156/q13/p3", "position": "The formula should be spoken for every harmful occurrence, including very small losses and remembered older ones.", "reasons": "The Prophet's extinguished lamp appears in Kashshāf, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, and Abū Ḥayyān; al-Qurṭubī and Ālūsī enumerate minor harms. The Commander of the Faithful, Ibn Mājah's report, and Ibn Kathīr say renewed istirjāʿ after a long time earns the original reward."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q14", "question": "Which parts of the response are obligatory or recommended?", "turns_on": "The notes address different prescribed acts: required submission, voluntary formula, and the added supplication.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q14/p1", "position": "Submission to God's command and decree, and continued duties, are obligatory; public verbal istirjāʿ is recommended.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr al-Rāzī distinguishes inner obedience from voluntary public utterance, which teaches others and displays steadfastness to disbelievers. Abū Ḥayyān repeats the distinction and says voicing it angers disbelievers by showing obedience and restraint."}, {"id": "2:156/q14/p2", "position": "After istirjāʿ, one should ask God for reward in the affliction and a better replacement.", "reasons": "Ālūsī expressly calls this recommended, citing Muslim's Umm Salama report. The reported prophetic instruction appears in Baghawī, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and Rāzī."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q15", "question": "Why teach believers to voice this declaration?", "turns_on": "Whether the stress falls on public teaching or the formula's consoling force.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q15/p1", "position": "Speech makes conviction vivid to the speaker and teaches witnesses to be steadfast.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a taught motto that strengthens belief by making it perceptible; Abū Bakr al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān say public recitation invites imitation and displays obedience to disbelievers. Jishumī likens it to reassuring the afflicted, 'I am yours.'"}, {"id": "2:156/q15/p2", "position": "Its wording intensifies acceptance and consoles the sufferer through God's just governance.", "reasons": "Jishumī says acknowledging an irresistible, just Lord prevents despair; Ṭabrisī says God repairs a deserved affliction or vindicates one unjustly harmed."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q16", "question": "What rewards are promised to those who say it patiently?", "turns_on": "The reports and commentators describe general blessings and specific forms of recompense.", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q16/p1", "position": "They receive divine blessings or forgiveness, mercy, and guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās lists all three from 2:157; Muqātil and Saʿīd b. Jubayr explain ṣalawāt as forgiveness, Muqātil comparing 9:103, while Saʿīd says mercy protects from punishment. ʿUmar calls blessing and mercy two equal portions with guidance as an extra topping. Al-Ṣādiq relates the three to those deprived of property by force; Biqāʿī says even minor calamities fall under the promise. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk connects eligibility with piety and fulfilling obligations. Ṭabrisī defines the promised guidance as attaining the true path."}, {"id": "2:156/q16/p2", "position": "God repairs the loss, gives a good outcome, and grants a pleasing righteous replacement.", "reasons": "Prophetic reports in Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Kashshāf, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, and al-Durr agree in this threefold promise; Qurṭubī says the glad tidings can be replacement, abundant reward, or both, exemplified by Umm Salama."}, {"id": "2:156/q16/p3", "position": "Particular losses may earn Paradise, a House of Praise, or elevated ranks.", "reasons": "Abū Mūsā's report promises a House of Praise when a bereaved parent praises God and recites istirjāʿ; al-Tirmidhī calls it ḥasan gharīb and identifies Abū Sinān as ʿĪsā ibn Sinān. Reports from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr and al-Ṣādiq promise a house or Paradise for four habits including istirjāʿ; Ali reports three hundred ranks for patient consolation, and Ibn ʿAmr promises Paradise for loss borne in hope of reward."}, {"id": "2:156/q16/p4", "position": "The formula turns apparent loss into provision saved with God and directs the sufferer toward what was lacking.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥarālī says return and surrendered losses become stored provision, faith in meeting God, and self-struggle; Bursawī similarly calls what God takes back provision held with Him. Biqāʿī says the speaker is guided toward what had fallen short."}]}
{"id": "2:156/q17", "question": "What incident with Umm Salama illustrates the prescribed supplication?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:156/q17/p1", "position": "After Abū Salama died, she recited istirjāʿ and asked for reward and a better replacement; God gave her the Prophet as husband.", "reasons": "Baghawī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and Ālūsī transmit the account.
